claims.text: The rollback-journal approach writes the original database content to a separate journal before changing the database file.
claims.quote: The traditional rollback journal works by writing a copy of the original unchanged database content into a separate rollback journal file and then writing changes directly into the database file.

claims.text: After a crash or rollback, SQLite uses the rollback journal to restore the original database content.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.

claims.text: A WAL transaction commits when SQLite appends a commit record to the WAL.
claims.quote: A COMMIT occurs when a special record indicating a commit is appended to the WAL.

claims.text: WAL commit can complete without writing to the database file, so readers can continue using the unaltered database while changes enter the WAL.
claims.quote: Thus a COMMIT can happen without ever writing to the original database, which allows readers to continue operating from the original unaltered database while changes are simultaneously being committed into the WAL.

claims.text: PASSIVE checkpoints do not wait for readers or writers and sync the database only if all log frames were checkpointed.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: FULL checkpoints wait until there is no writer and all readers use the latest database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: After those conditions hold, FULL checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: RESTART adds a wait until all readers use only the database file, so the next writer restarts the log from its beginning.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: TRUNCATE behaves like RESTART and truncates the log to zero bytes before a successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and can be used to retrieve the API output values.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: By default, SQLite checkpoints on a commit that brings the WAL to at least 1000 pages or when the final connection closes.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint configures checkpointing after commit when the WAL has at least N frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative N disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Concurrent checkpoint attempts can fail to acquire the exclusive checkpoint lock and return SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE also acquire the exclusive writer lock.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while waiting for the writer lock or readers, the checkpoint falls back to PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop before it reaches WAL content past the end mark of any current reader.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
claims.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.text: If overlapping readers ensure at least one reader is always active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps allow checkpoints to be attempted when no processes are reading the database.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: Checkpoint sync operations protect against database corruption after power loss or a hard reboot.
claims.quote: Checkpointing does require sync operations in order to avoid the possibility of database corruption following a power loss or hard reboot.

claims.text: SQLite syncs the WAL before transferring its content to the database and syncs the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=FULL, writers sync the WAL on each commit; with NORMAL, they omit that sync.
claims.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.

claims.text: With synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues a sync or I/O barrier.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Running checkpoints in another thread or process prevents the query and update thread from blocking on a sync operation.
claims.quote: If an application therefore runs checkpoint in a separate thread or process, the main thread or process that is doing database queries and updates will never block on a sync operation.

claims.text: Under this configuration, a power failure or hard reset can roll back transactions because they are not durable.
claims.quote: The downside to this configuration is that transactions are no longer durable and might rollback following a power failure or hard reset.

claims.text: Read performance declines as the WAL grows because readers check it for page content.
claims.quote: On the other hand, read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.

claims.text: Checkpoint page writes can include many seeks, making checkpoints slower than write transactions.
claims.quote: but even then there will typically be many seek operations interspersed among the page writes. These factors combine to make checkpoints slower than write transactions.

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints keep the WAL small and maximize read performance.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT.

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across writes but allow the WAL to grow larger.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.

claims.text: Checkpoints usually recycle the WAL by overwriting it from the beginning rather than truncating it, unless journal_size_limit is set.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: When the last connection closes, it checkpoints once and deletes the WAL and shared-memory files.
claims.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

claims.text: pnLog reports the total log-frame count, or -1 when the checkpoint cannot run because of an error or the database is not in WAL mode.
claims.quote: If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file or to -1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode.

claims.text: pnCkpt reports the total checkpointed-frame count, including frames checkpointed before the call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: SQLite WAL relies on shared memory, so readers must be on one machine and WAL does not work on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.
